A stack is the result totality of multiple technologies layered on top of one another. For web design, a common stack looks like this (lower means more foundational; you need these to use the ‘higher-level’ technology)

Client-Side scripting (javascript)

Layering and Styling (CSS)

Markup and Logical Positioning (HTML)

Page Pre-Processing (PHP, CGI, ASP)

Web Server (apache/IIS)

In the above example, the web server handles an incoming request from a client (i.e. someone accessing a page in a browser) and runs a program which loads a pre-processing script Like PHP and prepares the output (which is in HTML format) for the client. this output is given to the client whose browser renders the document as laid out by the markup/HTML, provides styling as per the CSS in the HTML document. After this is achieved, the browser attempts to find and load any active scripting defined by the HTML and run any loaded at the appropriate time defined by the script.

First, HTML isn’t a programming language, nor is it “code.” HTML is a markup language.

Programming languages are the steps that computers run; they are sets of instructions, like a recipe.

Code is a very overused term, let's avoid it.

Markup Languages are systems for "marking up" or annotating or putting information around other information, to change how that other information displays. Voat's comments have a small markup language; *BOLD* makes BOLD text, [link text](http://link.url), etc.

HTML (and its companion, CSS) are instructions to web browsers that answer the question "Okay, so, I should show the person the word "BOLD." What font should it be? How big should the letters be? What color should it be? Where should it be on the screen? etc, etc. Markup languages don't have any kind of recipe or instruction ability; they just add extra information to whatever they're marking up.

There have been many different specifications of "what is HTML?" over the years. The current thing to learn is the HTML5 specification. Same thing for CSS (Cascading Style Sheets - they typically address more of the "what should it look like?" aspect of a webpage, while HTML handles "what content is in the webpage") - CSS3 is the current revision to learn.

JavaScript is a programming language that runs in browsers and lets webpages do things that require some kind of programming language. HTML and CSS alone can't do that. Basic webpages don't need it.

Back when word processing first began, you used to have to add all of the formatting codes around the text so the device you were either printing or displaying the text on knew how to correctly print or display the text.

HTML is a lot like that. Basically you have your content - text info, pictures and movie links, whatever, and you have to format that content for how it is to be displayed in internet browsers. That includes stuff like color, font, spacing, lines, tables, etc. HTML has rules for how all of this is supposed to be done, and all of the browsers can read those pages, once they are properly formatted - or so they say - the devil, as always, is in the details.

So, if you want to start doing websites quickly, start with HTML, which is pretty easy, and build up your knowledge from there. It soon begins to get a lot more complicated as you expand your skill set.
